content:
Hi everyone!

I’m an undergraduate math student (currently studying pure math: analysis, algebra, topology). I've recently been fascinated by Lean 4 and its intersection with AI4Math. I've read through some parts of TPIL 4 and MIL, and I want to start a systematic project to truly do something.

My current idea is to try to independently formalize the theorems and exercises from my undergraduate point-set topology textbook.

I have a few questions and would love to hear your advice:

  1. Is this a solid milestone? Would successfully doing this be considered reaching a solid "entry-level" proficiency in Lean?

  2. Is this a recommended learning path? I know some areas of math are much harder to formalize than they appear on paper. I’ve vaguely heard that Mathlib uses Filters heavily for topology. As a beginner used to traditional open/closed sets, are there any specific pitfalls I should be aware of?

  3. Any alternative suggestions? If topology is too tricky for a first project, what area of undergraduate math would you recommend I formalize instead to build a strong foundation, or maybe I should just continue reading the last 7 chapters in MIL.

In all, I'm a bit lost about my learning and practice path in lean engineering, and I'd like to know what the best next step should be. Thanks in advance for any guidance!

If you are going to do this by hand (because you want to learn some Lean) -- this is a super project. I spent quite some time going through point set topology theorems in Lean when I was learning. I didn't use filters at all, I just proved all the theorems the way the proofs were in the books.

If you're going to use AI to do it -- this is arguably a complete waste of time and money. The answer is "AI can do it easily and I just spent some money on tokens and learnt nothing".

I would recommend not making any new definitions, and using the definitions in mathlib. Be careful not to "cheat" and type some tactic which just finds the proof in the library.

Hmm, I'm a little disappointed (with myself) that my work on topological spaces didn't make it into the Imperial undergraduate course: https://github.com/b-mehta/formalising-mathematics-notes/tree/main/FormalisingMathematics2026/Section11TopologicalSpaces will get you started with how to use topological spaces and continuous functions, but there's nothing like "compact subspace of a Hausdorff space is closed", an example I remember very fondly. Typing the proof into Lean made me realise that the proof used the axiom of choice in an essential way! Here is some information, but all in Lean 3 mind you, about how I was teaching this in 2021 https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2021/02/10/formalising-mathematics-workshop-4/ and here is the associated Lean 3 code https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/formalising-mathematics/blob/master/src/week_4/Part_C_topology.lean . Your first exercise is to translate the questions into Lean 4 and here you _could_ use an LLM to do this, because there's no point you wasting your time learning anything about Lean 3.

Note that in the traditional proof of "closed subset of compact is compact" you might want to say "I have a cover of this, and now I need a cover of that by using the cover of this and throwing in one more open set" and to do this in Lean you need to know how to extend an index set by one element. This is covered in one of the other files in https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/formalising-mathematics/tree/master/src/week_4 .

There are also a few cool video about topology in Xena summer stuff, by Kevin
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ygAl4PGFY0w&list=PLVZep5wTamMmvdvczjrLctDM9T4nBse1M&index=6

Just like learning to write any programming language, the answer is write a lot of code first, get very comfortable with the syntax, standard libraries, reading errors. Later focus on actual code style, architecture, performance, etc.

I was in a very similar boat around an year ago and found working through https://github.com/teorth/analysis companion helpful to level up my lean skills after TPIL and MIL. My solutions are https://github.com/rkirov/analysis and I have blogged about my learning journey here https://rkirov.github.io, you might find some of the posts useful. It is definitely a very good idea to write a bunch of lean proofs to get a feel for the language, tactics, reading through compiler errors etc.

I haven't done them, but I think the exercises in a basic point-set topology book like Munkres should be good fit. If you feel so inclined, you can even consider writing a lean companion text, so that others can play through them too - see #general > self-learning math with lean @ 💬 for a discussion on how to make more lean companions (Tao's is the only complete one I know of). But that is probably a harder than just doing the exercises, I hope to write some more eventually, maybe one day we can have a whole university math curriculum covered through lean companions.

Thank you all so much for the incredibly helpful suggestions, video links, and shared learning journeys!

I completely agree with the consensus on AI. My ultimate goal is to build genuine mathematical intuition from the ground up, so I will strictly write the proofs by hand and avoid using auto-tactics. However, using an LLM to translate the week 4 Lean 3 exercises into Lean 4 is a brilliant use of the tool, and I am diving into that exercise right away. I also really appreciate the specific heads-up about extending the index set for open covers—that’s the kind of technical pitfall I was learning about.

The advice to "write a lot of code first" to get comfortable with the syntax and compiler errors is exactly the mindset I need right now. Furthermore, the idea of eventually writing a "Lean companion" for an undergraduate topology textbook (like Munkres) is inspiring and a perfect long-term goal, but maybe it's a bit difficult for me now.

I'm going to start getting my hands dirty with the code now. Thanks again, everyone, and I'll report back once I make some solid progress!
